en: Chapter Thirty-one: The Ritual Manual for the *Abhicāruka* [Rite] of the Mantra of the Wrathful King Yamāntaka,
from the *Mahāvaipulya Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta-bodhisattva-puṣpavyūha-mūla-śāsana-stotra*.
Chapter Two: The Principal Deities of the Six Limbs; Chapter Thirty-one: Ritual Procedures.
At that time, the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, surveyed the great assembly and those seated in the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
The assembly addressed them thus:
"You all should listen to that which has been spoken by Mañjuśrī, the King of Wrath, whose majesty and ferocity are peerless."
To subdue those who are difficult to discipline,
even to the point of executing them so that they may submit and obey,
one shall first explain the ritual procedures for painting images.
At that time, the Lord of Secrets Vajrapāṇi spoke these words in verse:
"One need not select auspicious days or lunar mansions, nor is one restricted by fasting or ritual observances."
For one who fears enemies, one should paint an image of the Wrathful One on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or on the fourteenth day;
it should be taken from a cemetery and wrapped in the cloth of a deceased Brahmin.
During the middle watch of the night, one should soak the brush in blood and then wash it with water.
One must employ a fierce and wicked painter whose appearance is terrifying and who is prone to anger.
During the dark fortnight, in a cemetery, one should perform the rite for three nights so that it becomes eight or fourteen nights; having lit a lamp with dog fat,
the practitioner should draw a person and stand facing south.
Sitting upon a skull, protecting the mind and body, the practitioner may dwell there;
or he may draw it himself. When oppressed by terrifying enemies, during the first watch of the night, the bodies of those enemies shall burn.
In the second watch, they suffer from cold and heat; when possessed by spirits, they are all dazed and distressed.
In the third watch, they lose their lives; having died and gone to another world, how could they remain at ease while harboring malice toward the practitioner?
The bodies of their enemies shall wither and rot, and their families shall be exterminated.
By means of painting this image, [one achieves these results].
The image of Yamāntaka has six faces and twelve arms; it is black in color, with a belly like that of a wolf.
Wearing a garland of skulls and wrathful, he has a tiger skin for a lower garment and carries various weapons;
with hands joined in supplication, he is terrifying,
his eyes blood-red and his form violent and fierce, marked by three eyes as his emblem.
With upright hair blazing like flames, or with the color of black smoke like that of an asana flower;
having the hue of dark clouds during a summer rain,
his form is like the conflagration at the end of an eon— he should be depicted riding upon a water buffalo.
A wrathful and terrifying being, capable of destroying Raurava and severing the life of Yama; with fierce anger as his constant occupation,
he is utterly cruel and most formidable among the fearsome.
One who can slay all sentient beings should paint this wrathful deity using one's own blood as the pigment;
blending the colors with shades of light and dark,
mixed with dog fat and cow ghee, and placing them in a skull vessel.
Using hair from a corpse as a brush and a dog’s bone as a pen,
one should paint while observing the vow of fasting. One should personally offer,
or have others offer, extensive food, flowers, and the like, along with red garlands and sandalwood incense.
Dog meat is used as incense; human fat serves as the lamp for the time of solemnly painting a sacred image.
One should clearly perform the offerings at the beginning, middle, and end of the session to recompense the labor of the artist.
One should give generously and at a high price to make their hearts rejoice;
one should perform this immediately. When purchasing necessary goods for great and powerful undertakings, a hero does not haggle over the price.
Once the rite has been accomplished, one should reward the painter with various offerings to make him joyful and sever his expectations;
one must protect his person, for otherwise, he will suffer harm.
Together with their family and retinue, they shall also protect themselves;
one should visualize them while performing the recitation. This is the ritual procedure:
by clearly creating this image, one's heart's desires will be fulfilled as soon as it is seen.
To accomplish all tasks, one should carry the excellent image when facing violent enemies who cause harm;
likewise for those seeking great power according to their desires,
or for those who oppose kings, the wealthy, or the dissolute.
Especially those with overweening pride, persons of fierce and evil karma who do not benefit the Triple Gem,
those with nihilistic views who loathe mantras and show no respect for mantra-practitioners,
or those who harbor resentment toward those who revere them.
One should also perform rites for those who disparage practitioners of recitation, who treat mantras with contempt,
who perform rituals contrary to the rules, who never delight in wholesome dharmas,
and who afflict sentient beings. For their sake, one should perform the ritual.
Before long, his life shall come to an end. Take wood, bark, leaves, roots, and their fruits;
mix these with sour gruel, powdered human bone, mustard oil, and poison.
Take ginger and powdered red mustard seeds,
mix them entirely with human blood, and place them before the image;
the practitioner faces south, while the honored image faces north.
Before the image, one should perform the *kuṇḍa* ritual by kindling a fire with *kṛtavedhana* wood or burning its thorny wood; into that hearth,
one who is fully conversant with the ritual procedures should place the combined substances for the *homa* offering.
Then one should summon the Fire Deity; with the Wrathful Vidyārāja,
one should immediately form the Śūla-mudrā and offer [the oblation] into the fire one thousand and eight times for the accomplishment of all activities, performing them all as great wrathful acts.
First the child perishes; next the kinsmen die.
Second, the master and his wife perish, along with their relatives.
Third, they all die; this should be understood according to the teaching.
Before this image, one should recite at midnight in order to harm those enemies;
thus, one should act accordingly so that the kingdom shall perish and the military hosts be afflicted by pestilence.
Fire breaks out and great winds arise; torrential rains fall in deluges.
All the great hosts of the army face the enemy coming to punish them;
various calamities and all manner of diseases break out.
All bodies shall wither and waste away; there is no doubt that this is brought about by that rebellious king.
Non-human spirits will fill his home, and amidst constant strife and contention, he shall find no peace in sleep or rest.
The earth shakes all around; rākṣasas suck their vital energy.
They surround their homes, afflicting them with terror and distress, leading to agonizing suffering. No one is able to protect them.
The Īśvaras and other earth-deities, Brahmā and the other world-protectors,
Śakra, lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, all the mantra-deities,
and all the gods of the world— as soon as they see [him], they manifest wrath.
His life shall instantly perish; whether at midnight or at midday,
if the reciter becomes angry, King Yama himself will cause his body to tremble and split asunder, according to his pleasure during the dark fortnight.
Having consecrated this honored image, one should extensively perform offerings;
dwelling in wildernesses or among burial mounds, by solitary trees, at *liṅga* shrines, in mountains,
or within mountain caves, one should live alone without companions.
One should always perform this rite in a tranquil great forest,
in the midst of the empty sky, in an empty cave,
or by the side of a river or the seashore; one should go to such places as these.
Abiding there according to one's inclination, within a range of a hundred yojanas,
one should perform this rite in such a manner; having spoken thus,
it should be performed with purity regarding its dimensions, and one should remain heedful.
The realm of mantras is inconceivable; The practice of mantras is inconceivable;
The spiritual powers of mantras are inconceivable; The accomplishments of the practitioner are inconceivable;
The activities performed are inconceivable; The karmic fruits obtained are inconceivable.
Now manifest as the Wrathful King Yamāntaka, born from the supernatural power of great majesty and karma, he sports within the realm of supernatural powers.
Having accomplished inconceivable feats, the practitioner appears here in Jambudvīpa; such is the great majesty of all Bodhisattvas.
None of them have the power to provide protection— how much less so the various mantras of the world,
all the grahas, the Mātṛs, Īśāna and the others, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva,
Kumāra, and even Śakra, the Lord of the Devas.
By means of the samaya, one is able to protect those sons of the Buddha and bodhisattvas,
as well as pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas who abide in the ten stages through their majestic power— those of great majesty who are free from desire.
Unable to protect or uphold that which was originally sought as their primary vow, I shall now briefly proclaim it: listen!
Those who seek wealth and status will bring harm to the practitioner; there is no one capable of restraining them.
If one does not delight in the vidyādhara, how can calamities be pacified?
If one gives rise to pure faith and also generates a mind of compassion,
and recites the King of Wrathful Deities, the Greatly Majestic Yamāntaka.
At that time, calamities are dispelled, and one’s own life is protected:
white mustard seeds, oil, the five types of *vatsanābha* medicine,
dog blood, and dog meat, the three pungents, salt, and mustard seeds.
Śaṅkha-puṣpī, amlavetasa, samudra-lavaṇa,
dhattūra, and kuśumbha; the root of priyaṅgu, hemp ash,
the root of red safflower, kaṇṭakārī, and madana-root.
Onions, garlic, *pāṭala* flowers, *kuṭaja*, leeks, *sūraṇa*,
and medicinal liquor— having thus divided these substances equally,
one should cast them into the furnace before the image and burn them for one thousand and eight times.
The lineage of enemies shall perish; kinsmen and friends, the protectors of heaven and their retinues—all shall be utterly eradicated.
As for the second round, the reciter performs the homa.
Then that land and its territories, along with its towns and villages,
shall all suffer from famine, drought, and pestilence; they shall be filled with rākṣasas,
and there shall be fires, rains of stones, thunderbolts, frost, and hail.
In villages and hamlets, and even throughout the king’s realm,
much affliction arises; enemy armies come to punish that land,
bringing forth calamities and portents of every kind of inauspiciousness.
If one burns the roots of *dudura*, that person will immediately become insane;
if one constantly burns pungent and sharp substances, the entire body will feel as if it is being consumed by fire;
if one burns extremely sour substances, one will be afflicted with alternating fever and chills.
Born within that body, those who are rebellious toward the king,
arrogant, part of a great faction, and violent— supported by a vast host of followers—
for two nights or seven nights, they shall cause their lives to end completely.
The deity whom that person serves, along with its attendant constellations—
having reduced them to ashes for the cremation of the corpse—
one should completely assume their forms before the honored image and trample upon their heads with one’s feet.
While reciting the mantra, one should remain in a wrathful state,
causing that rebellious and deceitful king to be suddenly afflicted by various kinds of diseases. Overwhelmed by these great maladies,
he shall perish in an instant, dying from the bites of fierce beasts.
Some have their limbs severed; others are devoured by rākṣasas,
impure non-humans, flesh-eating piśācas, pūtanas, pretas, and the mātṛs.
One’s own body and attendants perish in an instant; Vajrapāṇi,
the Holder of Auspiciousness, having spoken while amidst the assembly and paid homage to all Buddhas, remains in silent composure.
For the benefit of the world, he further spoke these words:
"All the hosts of yakṣas, the yakṣiṇīs, the mantras spoken by bodhisattvas, and the yakṣa generals and lords."
The Wheel of the Yakṣiṇī Teachings: For those who seek defilement through mantras—
Who summon and practice love at will, Yet fail to dispel all afflictions—
Their wisdom is clouded by the darkness of craving.
Unable to apply the antidotes, they are restrained by the Buddha’s precepts;
having practiced [evil] throughout beginningless saṃsāra, they are deeply pitiable.
From suffering to further suffering, the Buddha therefore spoke of the evil destinies.
If one can guard the sense faculties, one attains the holy life and a fortunate rebirth;
therefore, the virtuous and tranquil one ultimately realizes nirvāṇa.
By means of the equality of the three karmas, one attains parinirvāṇa.
Inverted and swallowing unwholesome wisdom, the foolish are stained by the darkness of birth and death within the dense forest of evil. Wandering through the five destinies,
out of compassion for their suffering, listen to this which overcomes greed and defilement.
It can obstruct all transgressions and sever the three kinds of faults;
by reverently following the teachings of the Dharma King, one is liberated from all fetters and bonds.

32. Chapter on the Wrathful Kings, from the *Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta-bodhisattva-avaivartika-cakra-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-two: The Chapter on the Wrathful King Yamāntaka. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati...
Seated within that great assembly,
he rose from his seat, prostrated before all the Tathāgatas,
and remained within the gathering.
He circumambulated Śākyamuni Buddha three times,
took hold of the Buddha’s two feet, and knelt reverently for a long time;
he then beheld Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas.
He spoke these words:
"You are exceedingly violent and evil!
Vajrapāṇi acts for the sake of all sentient beings."
To preach the killing of all sentient beings and to listen to the mantra teachings on all forms of lustful passion—
O Son of the Buddha, such is not the dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
Now, as for the great Bodhisattvas:
they are born from great compassion and practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva for the benefit of others.
Because they practice with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*),
they are not separated from the bonds of existence.
O Son of the Buddha, such is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He teaches all sentient beings those dharmas that harm other sentient beings;
for he has accomplished great compassion and possesses the superior intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying: "Śāntamati,
a bodhisattva should train in this way and abide in this way."
Just as you have said and just as you have demonstrated,
and just as all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of great majestic power have spoken, so too do I speak.
Based on the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is thus said:
The ultimate reality is inconceivable; Maturation is inconceivable;
The Buddha-dharmas are inconceivable; The Bodhisattva is inconceivable.
The conduct for subduing sentient beings, the inconceivable practice of the practices—this is the conduct of Bodhisattvas; therefore it is called "inconceivable.
Regarding all the teachings of mantras, their majestic power is inconceivable.
The Mantra of the Wrathful King: The Greatly Majestic Yamāntaka possesses inconceivable supernormal powers;
together with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas such as the Greatly Majestic and Inconceivable Śāntimati and others.
In this same way, O Śāntamati, a bodhisattva who practices mantras should generate such a mind regarding the realm of sentient beings.
If one engages in sexual misconduct,
one incurs immeasurable sin against all sentient beings and falls into the great hell of Avīci.
If one harbors anger toward sentient beings,
one incurs immeasurable sin;
do not allow sentient beings to become incapable of attaining the three types of enlightenment.
Śāntamati, a bodhisattva who maintains the mantra in this way gives rise to such a thought:
"By means of skillful expedients, I..."
When performing ābhicāruka rites,
one should not grasp at signs nor cling to what is unwholesome in any ritual activity.
One should train in the skillful means for taming sentient beings,
with a mind enveloped by great compassion.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, there are what are called "Dharma" and "non-Dharma."
Pure and impure;
wholesome and unwholesome;
skillful in responding to and transforming sentient beings.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas flow forth from the dharmadhātu;
they practice the teachings and then skillfully expound those very teachings to sentient beings.
One should dwell correctly in this manner for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha, we should train ourselves thus:
namely, by disciplining sentient beings, maturing sentient beings, and pacifying sentient beings.
All those sons of the Buddha who enter this maṇḍala assembly should listen with pure faith and properly examine what is wholesome and unwholesome; that is to say,
they should generate deep love and joy for the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata and must not harbor doubt or slander.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati observed the inconceivable nature of the Buddha-dharma and remained silent.
With such a mental orientation, he gazed up at the Tathāgata.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets,
surveyed the assembled multitude and again proclaimed the teachings of the Wrathful Kings.
He addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O you hosts of devas and the spirits who are the support for the realm of sentient beings,
practitioners should first protect their own bodies."
Take an image of the Wrathful King and place it in a single location—
namely, in a temple of Maheśvara Liṅga—
and [apply] poison, mustard seeds, and dog blood.
They smear themselves with fermented gruel-water.
There is an *ṛṣi* who takes white *bhañja* leaves as an offering and uses human intestines as a divine cord.
He wraps it with crossed bands.
Holding a human skull in his right hand,
he hurls and strikes it against the liṅga.
With the index finger of his left hand raised in great wrath,
he stands confronting that rebellious king who treats others with contempt,
as well as other evil persons, great factions, and violent, malevolent lords.
As for the place where the ritual is performed:
close the door, go naked, and let your hair hang loose;
then, with your left foot, step upon the *liṅga* of Maheśvara.
Torn asunder into two pieces,
one should not feel fear upon hearing the great sound of HŪṂ;
on that very day, the king and his other wicked factions and enemies will be overthrown.
Then one will be afflicted by a severe fever or chills,
or possessed by a non-human (*amanuṣya*) or a *rākṣasa*.
Furthermore, one must continue reciting for a brief moment.
Their enemies will perish in an instant.
If one recites it until dawn,
the family members of that person will be destroyed.
Furthermore, at midday, go to a temple of Maheśvara,
take *kaṭuka* leaves and offer them;
burn dog meat as incense and recite the mantra.
That enemy will be consumed by fire and immediately afflicted with a malarial fever that causes shivering.

If one dwells without interruption in a state of wrath upon the right side of Mahesvara’s body,
that very enemy will perish; if one wishes for them to be restored as before, [one should perform the following].
Furthermore, he washed Liṅga with water and bathed it with cold cow’s milk;
it returned to its former state as before.
Furthermore, there is another method: on the right side of Maheśvara Liṅga,
one should burn fuel of *madanaka* thorny wood and *vibhītaka* wood.
Obtain poisonous blood and mustard oil;
cast them into the fire one thousand and eight times.
Then that enemy will be afflicted with a grave illness for which no medical treatment can avail.
On the second day, they are seized by great diseases of cold or heat, or by major illnesses;
or they are afflicted by various ailments or possessed by non-human spirits, leading to death.
On the third day, at the three periods [of the day], they recite the mantra, yet their lives are entirely forfeited.
If one desires to restore things to their former state,
by performing *homa* with milk for that village and its enemies,
all shall attain peace and happiness.
In this manner, one should step upon all the deities and all the spirits to whom that person offers service while reciting the mantra;
one should also write down the constellation (nakṣatra) to which that person belongs.
Step upon it with the left foot.
With the exception of the mantras spoken by the Tathāgata,
one should perform the ritual and recite all other worldly mantras by stepping over them with the big toe of the left foot.
Without requiring prior cultivation or accomplishment,
merely by reciting it, the Wrathful King can accomplish all activities.
It can also destroy all mantras, harm all enemies, and shatter all mantra-dharmas.
I shall now explain this briefly.
Following the practitioners' reliance upon the ritual manuals (vidhi) of all mundane and supramundane mantras,
even if it is not explicitly stated in the root teaching [it should be applied].
Even by taking [mantras] from other sections, one still attains all accomplishments;
merely by reciting, one can fulfill all wishes;
merely by reciting the King of Wrath.
One attains the supreme siddhi;
by generating the mind according to one's wishes, one is also able to subdue all adversaries.
This is performed in conjunction with the binding of the śūla-mudrā.
This accomplishes all undertakings.
Furthermore, at noon, one should go to a charnel ground where corpses are burned and fast for one day and one night.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
take wood from a charnel ground to kindle a fire;
then mix poison, mustard seeds, and blood together.
Recite the mantra once and burn [the offering] once;
immediately the sound "ha ha" will be heard,
and all the hungry ghosts (preta) will arrive.

In this way, all various types of activities and *siddhis* can be accomplished.
Furthermore, according to another method, one should take white mustard seeds and recite the mantra in a pure, secluded, and tranquil place.
Recite the mantra one thousand and eight times for each burning.

take some of the ashes and divide a piece of clean cloth into two parts.

wrap them inside a ceramic bowl and cover it with another ceramic bowl.

place two vessels before you. Naked,
with disheveled hair, and with a wrathful mind free from fear.

by consecrating the object with this, one will achieve success.
